```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5,
                      dpi = 72, out.width = "100%")
```

The previous vignettes used discrete distributions (ratings on a 1-7 scale).
This one shows how **DistrViz** handles **histogram data**, i.e. the `MatH`
objects of the **HistDAWass** package, where each cell is the empirical
distribution of a continuous variable.

```{r}
library(DistrViz)
library(HistDAWass)
library(ggplot2)
```

## The data

`China_Month` (in **HistDAWass**) contains, for 60 meteorological stations of
China, the histograms of several climatic variables for each month, built
from the monthly records of many years. We start with the **mean monthly
temperatures** (°C): a table of 60 stations × 12 months, where each cell is
the distribution of the mean temperature of that month across the years.

```{r}
vars <- paste0("mean.temp_", month.abb)
Temp <- China_Month[, match(vars, colnames(China_Month@M))]
colnames(Temp@M) <- month.abb
rownames(Temp@M) <- sub("_[0-9]+$", "", rownames(Temp@M))   # drop the station codes
Temp[1:4, 1:3]
```

(Columns are selected by their *index*: `match()` turns the names into
positions.)

## From histograms to colours: `n_levels`

To be drawn, each histogram is turned into a discrete distribution: the range
of the variable is split into `n_levels` classes of equal width and each class
gets the probability that the histogram gives to it
(`DDAWASS::MatH2MatD()`). The $k$-th class gets the colour position
$u = (k - 1)/(n_\text{levels} - 1)$, so the first class has the colour of the
low end of the palette and the last one the colour of the high end.

```{r}
dv <- dv_data(Temp, n_levels = 15, scheme = "global")
dv
```

The class bounds are stored in the object (and shown in the tooltips of the
interactive heatmaps):

```{r}
round(dv$breaks$Jan, 1)
```

`n_levels` sets the resolution of the picture: few classes give a coarse,
"posterized" picture, many classes a smooth one. 10-20 classes are usually
a good compromise.

```{r, fig.width = 3.4, fig.height = 3.6, out.width = "48%", fig.show = "hold"}
gei_plot(Temp, row = "HaErBin", n_levels = 5, scheme = "global",
         palette = "Blue-Red 3", title = "HaErBin, 5 classes")
gei_plot(Temp, row = "HaErBin", n_levels = 30, scheme = "global",
         palette = "Blue-Red 3", title = "HaErBin, 30 classes")
```

## The annual cycle in a Green Eyes plot

With the twelve months as sectors, a Green Eyes plot becomes a **clock**:
January is at the top and the months follow clockwise. We use a diverging
blue-red palette, and the global scheme so that the same colour means the same
temperature in all the months. Here are twelve stations, ordered from north
to south using the coordinates in `stations_coordinates`:

```{r}
lat <- with(stations_coordinates, LAT.deg + LAT.min / 60)
names(lat) <- rownames(Temp@M)
sel <- c("Hailaer", "HaErBin", "HuHeHaoTe", "BeiJing", "LanZhou", "LaSa",
         "XiAn", "ShangHai", "ChengDu", "KunMing", "GuangZhou", "HaiKou")
sel <- sel[order(-lat[sel])]
```

```{r, fig.height = 3.6}
gei_grid(dv, rows = sel, ncol = 6, palette = "Blue-Red 3")
```

(The same eyes with the white fixed at 0 °C are obtained with the `ranges`
argument, see below.)

Northern stations have deep blue winters (the blue band starts at the
pupil: the whole distribution is below zero) and a sharp contrast with the
summer; going south the winter sectors turn white and then red, and in HaiKou
(Hainan island) the eye is red all around. LaSa (Lhasa, 3650 m) and KunMing
(1890 m) have mild summers because of their altitude.

### The calendar is the shortest Hamiltonian cycle

The order of the months was taken from the calendar. Would an automatic order
find it? `dv_var_order()` looks for the shortest Hamiltonian cycle through the
variables, using the correlation distance $\sqrt{2(1-r)}$ between the
Wasserstein correlations of the months:

```{r}
dv_var_order(Temp)$labels
```

The cycle found is exactly the annual cycle: each month is most correlated
with the previous and the following one, and December closes the circle with
January. With 12 variables the cycle is found heuristically (exact enumeration
is used up to 9 variables).

## Colour schemes

The `scheme` argument of `dv_data()` (and of all the plotting functions)
decides how the classes are defined:

* `"variable"` (default): each variable has its own range. Colours show
  where a distribution lies **with respect to the other units on the same
  variable**: a red January is a warm January, even if it is colder than a
  blue July.
* `"global"`: one range for all the variables. Colours have the same meaning
  everywhere; this is the natural choice when all the variables are measured on
  the same scale, as the temperatures here.
* `"standardized"`: each variable is standardized with its Wasserstein mean
  and standard deviation and the classes span $\pm 3$ standard deviations.
  This is the choice for variables measured on **different scales**.

The difference between the first two schemes is clear in a heatmap. With
`scheme = "global"` (and without reordering the months) the annual cycle
dominates the picture; the legend reports the temperatures, since the range is
common to all the months. Note that the white of the diverging palette is at
the middle of the observed range (about -2 °C), not at 0 °C.

```{r, fig.height = 8.5}
dist_heatmap(dv, cluster_cols = FALSE, palette = "Blue-Red 3", label_size = 7)
```

To fix the classes, give `dv_data()` the `ranges` argument: the range is split
into `n_levels` classes of equal width. With a range symmetric around 0 and an
odd number of classes, the central class is centred on 0 °C and gets the white
of the palette: blue now means *below freezing*. Here 19 classes of 4 °C
cover $[-38, 38]$ °C.

```{r, fig.height = 8.5}
dv0 <- dv_data(Temp, n_levels = 19, ranges = c(-38, 38))
dist_heatmap(dv0, cluster_cols = FALSE, palette = "Blue-Red 3", label_size = 7)
```

With `scheme = "variable"` each month is compared with the same month in the
other stations: the annual cycle disappears and the geographical contrasts
(north-south, coast-inland, altitude) come out within each month.

```{r, fig.height = 8.5}
dist_heatmap(Temp, n_levels = 15, scheme = "variable", cluster_cols = FALSE,
             palette = "Blue-Red 3", label_size = 7)
```

### Variables on different scales

Let us now take six different variables measured in summer (from
`China_Seas`, the seasonal version of the data): temperature (°C),
precipitation (mm), relative humidity (%), sunshine duration (hours), wind
speed (m/s) and cloud amount (%).

```{r}
vs <- c("mean.temp_Summer", "tot.precip_Summer", "mean.rel.hum_Summer",
        "sunshine.dur_Summer", "mean.wind.speed_Summer", "mean.cloud.amount_Summer")
Summer <- China_Seas[, match(vs, colnames(China_Seas@M))]
colnames(Summer@M) <- c("temperature", "precipitation", "humidity", "sunshine",
                        "wind", "clouds")
rownames(Summer@M) <- rownames(Temp@M)
```

A global range would make no sense here (precipitation, in hundreds of
millimetres, would squeeze all the other variables into the first class). The
standardized scheme centres the palette on the Wasserstein mean of each
variable: yellow is "average", blue is below and red above the mean, by up to 3
standard deviations.

```{r, fig.height = 8.5}
dist_heatmap(Summer, n_levels = 12, scheme = "standardized", palette = "Zissou 1",
             label_size = 7)
```

With the default distance between variables, $\sqrt{1 - r^2}$, strongly
*anti*-correlated variables are close as well as correlated ones: sunshine
and cloud amount ($r = -0.80$) join first, then humidity and precipitation are
added, while wind, almost uncorrelated with the others, joins last. Use
`col_dist = "1-r"` to keep negatively correlated variables apart.

```{r}
round(WH.correlation(Summer), 2)
```

The first split of the stations separates the drier and sunnier summers from
the wetter and cloudier ones. The cluster means of the six variables (the means
of the histograms) make it explicit:

```{r}
hm <- dist_heatmap(Summer, n_levels = 12, scheme = "standardized")
k <- cutree(attr(hm, "clustering")$hc_rows, 2)
m <- get.MatH.stats(Summer, stat = "mean")$mat
round(aggregate(m, list(cluster = k), mean), 1)
split(names(k), k)
```

The first group collects the north-east, the north-west and some inland
stations of the south-east (e.g. NanChang, ChangSha); the second the coastal,
southern and south-western stations.

## Clustering the original or the discretized histograms

The dendrograms of `dist_heatmap()` (and the orderings of `gei_grid()` with
`order = "cluster"`) are computed by default on the **original histograms**
(`cluster_on = "source"`), with `HistDAWass::WH_hclust()` for the rows and
`HistDAWass::WH.correlation()` for the columns. The drawn picture is an
approximation of the data, but the clustering is not affected by it. With
`cluster_on = "discretized"` the clustering is computed on the discretized
distributions, i.e. on exactly what is drawn. With a reasonable number of
classes the two partitions are very similar:

```{r}
cl_src <- dv_cluster(dv_data(Temp, n_levels = 15, scheme = "global"))
cl_dis <- dv_cluster(dv_data(Temp, n_levels = 15, scheme = "global"), on = "discretized")
table(source = cutree(cl_src$hc_rows, 4), discretized = cutree(cl_dis$hc_rows, 4))
```

The clustering results can also be used outside **DistrViz**: here the four
clusters of stations are drawn on a map.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.5, out.width = "85%", fig.align = "center"}
coords <- data.frame(station = rownames(Temp@M),
                     lon = with(stations_coordinates, LON.deg + LON.min / 60),
                     lat = lat,
                     cluster = factor(cutree(cl_src$hc_rows, 4)))
ggplot(coords, aes(lon, lat, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  labs(x = "longitude", y = "latitude",
       title = "Ward clustering of the monthly temperature histograms") +
  theme_minimal()
```

and the eyes of all the stations, grouped by cluster:

```{r, fig.height = 12}
gei_grid(dv, groups = cutree(cl_src$hc_rows, 4), ncol = 6, palette = "Blue-Red 3")
```

## Stations on the factorial plane

Finally, `gei_pca()` puts each eye at the position of the station on the first
factorial plane of the quantile-based MFA of the twelve months
(`HistDAWass::WH.MultiplePCA()`). Each eye has a diameter equal to one tenth
of the smallest side of the cloud of points.

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
gei_pca(dv0, palette = "Blue-Red 3", label_size = 2)
```

The key on the right is the eye of the barycenter of the 60 stations
(the Wasserstein barycenter of the histograms of each month, discretized with
the same classes as the eyes): it tells which month is in each sector. With the
four clusters found above, `key = "groups"` draws the prototype (barycenter) of
each cluster instead, and the outline of every eye takes the colour of its
cluster:

```{r, fig.height = 5.5}
gei_pca(dv0, palette = "Blue-Red 3", label_size = 2,
        groups = cutree(cl_src$hc_rows, 4), key = "groups")
```

The prototypes summarise four climates: the coldest stations of the north
and north-east (blue winters: Heilongjiang, Jilin, Inner Mongolia, Urumqi), the
rest of the north and north-west (winters around or below 0 °C), the centre
and south-west, and the warm south.

The first axis is the north-south (cold-warm) gradient, from the deep blue
winters of Heilongjiang and Inner Mongolia on the left to the tropical south on
the right. The second axis isolates the high-altitude stations of the
south-west (LaSa, XiNing, KunMing, TengChong, XiChang), whose winters are mild
for their latitude and whose summers are cool.

With 60 stations the eyes overlap and the names are hard to read: the
interactive version (`interactive = TRUE`, it needs the **ggiraph** package)
shows the name of a station when the mouse is over its eye, hides an eye with a
click (leaving its point of application, in red; a click on the point shows it
again), hides the eyes of a whole area with the lasso, zooms on a part of the
plane, and has two switches (median circles, names) and a slider for the size
of all the eyes:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gei_pca(dv0, palette = "Blue-Red 3", label_size = 2,
        groups = cutree(cl_src$hc_rows, 4), interactive = TRUE,
        hidden = "HaiKou")
```

(Not run here: an interactive example is in the vignette on Green Eyes plots.)

## Stations on a map

The coordinates given to `gei_pca()` do not have to come from a factorial
analysis: any matrix with two columns, one row per unit, can be used. With the
longitude and the latitude of the stations, and a map drawn under the eyes
(`basemap`, a data frame of polygons such as those returned by
`ggplot2::map_data()`, which needs the **maps** package), each eye is centred
on its station. The dashed axes of the factorial plane are not drawn,
`axis_titles` names the axes, and `key_position` puts the key in an empty
corner of the map instead of in a box on the right.

```{r, eval = requireNamespace("maps", quietly = TRUE), fig.height = 6.2}
lonlat <- with(stations_coordinates,
               cbind(longitude = LON.deg + LON.min / 60, latitude = LAT.deg + LAT.min / 60))
rownames(lonlat) <- rownames(Temp@M)
china <- ggplot2::map_data("world", region = c("China", "Taiwan"))
gei_pca(dv0, lonlat, basemap = china, axis_titles = c("longitude", "latitude"),
        palette = "Blue-Red 3", size = 0.07, label_size = 1.8,
        key_position = c(80, 23), key_size = 0.22)
```

The map shows at once the latitudinal gradient (from the blue winters of the
north-east to the red eyes of the south coast and of Hainan), the effect of
the distance from the sea (Jiu Quan, in the north-west at the same latitude as
Beijing, has a January mean of -9.3 °C against -4.8 °C) and of altitude (the
eyes of LaSa and KunMing are paler than those of their neighbours: their July
means are 15.5 °C and 19.8 °C, against 25.8 °C in ChengDu and 28.5 °C in
NanNing).

The interactive version works on maps too: the tooltips report the longitude
and the latitude, and the slider enlarges all the eyes around their stations.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
gei_pca(dv0, lonlat, basemap = china, axis_titles = c("longitude", "latitude"),
        palette = "Blue-Red 3", size = 0.07, key_position = c(80, 23),
        key_size = 0.22, interactive = TRUE)
```
